title: Fine units or rich units
statement: Whether spaced review should keep fine-grained knowledge units and group them, or merge them into fewer, richer units.
example: One math curriculum's ~1,500 skills were collapsed into 427 knowledge units with 658 prerequisite links, and the complexity moved into each unit.
detail: A knowledge-graph BrainLift in the reading project's knowledge store finds that a fine-grained graph works for first teaching and remediation but makes retrieval scheduling unwieldy, and that there is one proven response and one speculative alternative, with no clear winner (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0116-graph-architecture-brainlift-core.qmd`). The proven response cuts the number of atoms, which moves the complexity into each one; the alternative keeps fine atoms and groups them into clusters for retrieval (the same file).

evidence.quote: There is one proven response and one speculative alternative, and it is not yet clear which is better.
collapsing Math Academy's ~1,500 skills into 427 atoms with far cleaner prerequisite chains (658 edges vs thousands).
This works, but the complexity does not disappear — it moves.
An alternative is to keep the fine-grained atoms but aggregate them into clusters for retrieval purposes
